author: Russell Brand
description:
Alex Jones reveals to Russell Brand the deeply personal spiritual ritual he has maintained every single day for over three years. Every night regardless of what time he goes to sleep Alex wakes up at 3am sharp, turns his phone off, dims the lights and sits alone at his coffee table for an hour in what he calls meditation but describes more accurately as waiting for God's orders. He asks the Holy Spirit what to do, how to fight and what God's mission is and then simply listens. Russell immediately points out that Alex probably should not be smoking a cigarette while receiving divine orders. Funny, surprising and deeply sincere.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell Brand reacts to a viral moment where a reporter attempts to trip Trump up over an AI generated image of him dressed as the Pope that was posted on the official White House account. Rather than taking the bait Trump dismantles the premise of the question entirely, points out that the Catholics loved it, notes that his wife thought it was cute, jokes that he would not be able to stay married if he became Pope and then simply tells the visibly deflated reporter to give him a break. Russell watches in admiration as Trump turns what was meant to be a gotcha moment into one of his most effortlessly funny press conference moments yet.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell Brand breaks down the fundamental flaw in representative democracy using a brilliantly simple analogy. The moment your elected representative leaves your village on his horse to go represent you in parliament or Congress someone is already waiting on the road to buy him. Before he even arrives your voice has been captured and co-opted by corporate and private interests. Russell argues this is not a bug in the system it is the system and that the only thing those in power truly fear is direct peer to peer communication and transaction between an awakened population that no longer needs a middleman to speak for them.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell Brand makes the case that centralized government has already comprehensively failed ordinary people and that endlessly debating which party or individual is better is a deliberate distraction from the real problem. Whether it is Republican or Democrat Labour or Conservative the institutions themselves are so thoroughly penetrated and controlled by big business and corporate interests that the fluctuation between political parties produces no meaningful change for ordinary people. Russell argues we must stop fetishizing or demonizing individual politicians and start addressing the systemic corruption of the container itself because until we do we will be trapped in an endless and manufactured conflict that serves the powerful perfectly.
